classification.summary: Found nortriptyline reduced depression but produced no clear superiority over placebo for tinnitus measures, and observed substantial placebo-arm improvements and measurement issues in tinnitus trials.
classification.key_finding: Placebo arm had ~32% reporting tinnitus improvement while nortriptyline reduced Hamilton Depression scores significantly; tinnitus-specific measures did not differ between drug and placebo.

title: An evaluation of three elements of pulmonary rehabilitation.
abstract: In this study of 39 patients with severe chronic airflow limitation, an independent group design examined the effect on exercise performance of a six-week program of leg muscle training, inspiratory muscle training and postural drainage. Exercise performance was reassessed at three months after the completion of the training program. MANOVA analysis of the 12-minute walking distance test showed a significant training effect (p < 0.001) with the largest effect occurring with leg muscle training (873 to 952 metres), a placebo response with postural drainage (886 to 925 metres) and minimal change with inspiratory muscle training (911 to 920 metres). There was a carry over effect at three months with leg muscle training, that was not seen in the other groups.

screening.rationale: Empirical study of pulmonary rehabilitation reported a 'placebo response' for postural drainage (improvement in placebo/sham arm), so placebo/nocebo phenomena were an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Tested three elements of pulmonary rehabilitation in 39 patients with severe chronic airflow limitation and found leg muscle training improved 12-minute walk distance, postural drainage produced a placebo response, and inspiratory muscle training produced minimal change.
classification.key_finding: Postural drainage produced a placebo-like improvement in 12-minute walk distance (886 to 925 m), while leg muscle training showed the largest gain (873 to 952 m).

title: Idebenone in the treatment of multi-infarct dementia: a randomised, double-blind, placebo controlled multicentre trial.
abstract: A controlled double blind randomised open multicentre study was carried out on 104 patients with multi-infarct dementia (MID) from a mild to a moderate degree. The patients were randomly assigned to balanced blocks in each center and treated for 90 days either with idebenone (CV-2619) 90 mg/daily or placebo, after a 2-week turn-in period. The Gottfries Rating Scale, SCAG, Rey's A Figure Test, Rey's 15 Words Test, Token Test, Verbal Fluidity Test and the Blessed Dementia Test were used for assessment. The data were statistically analyzed using parametric and non-parametric tests. Seven patients were excluded (5 idebenone + 2 placebo) after a few days treatment, for reasons not related to drug administration; therefore, 97 patients were assessed for efficacy and 104 for tolerability. A certain placebo effect was found in the examination results but it never achieved the efficacy levels of idebenone. The latter is particularly effective for improving recent and remote memory, attention, orientation, vigilance and verbal comprehension and the effects continued even after a month of placebo treatment. There were no important adverse reactions and neither laboratory parameters nor clinical vital signs were significantly altered.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial that reported and discussed a measurable placebo effect/placebo-arm improvement on cognitive outcomes, so placebo response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial in multi-infarct dementia found idebenone superior to placebo, but observed a measurable placebo-related improvement on cognitive tests.
classification.key_finding: Idebenone produced greater improvement on memory, attention, orientation and language tests, while the placebo arm showed some improvement but not to the same degree.

title: Expected effect of caffeine on motor performance predicts the type of response to placebo.
abstract: Two experiments (N = 56) investigated the relationship between subjects' expectancies concerning the effect of caffeine on a motor skill, and the type of placebo response. Male subjects were assigned to four groups. Three groups expected to receive caffeine but received a placebo. Prior to the placebo, two of the groups received information about the effect of caffeine on a motor skill task which led one group E(+) to expect enhanced performance, and the other E(-) to expect impairment. The third placebo group received no information E(?). A control group E(0) received no beverage, so neither caffeine nor any effect on performance was expected. The expected type of effect predicted the type of placebo response displayed. Group E(+) displayed greater improvement under placebo than did group E(0), and group E(-) performed more poorly than those in group E(0). No placebo response was observed in group E(?). Placebo effects on mood were correlated with subjects' predictions about the effect of caffeine on mood. The role of expectancies in response to placebos and psychoactive drugs is discussed.

screening.rationale: Included because the study experimentally manipulated expectancy and compared placebo beverage groups to a no-beverage control, directly testing placebo effects on motor performance and mood.

classification.summary: Tested expectancy manipulations about caffeine in healthy male volunteers and found that expecting enhancement produced performance gains under placebo, expecting impairment produced worse performance, and mood placebo effects tracked expectancy.
classification.key_finding: Expecting caffeine-induced improvement produced greater placebo improvement vs no-beverage control, while expecting impairment produced performance decrements (N=56).

title: Methodology of measuring the efficacy of antidepressants.
abstract: Evaluation of the efficacy of antidepressant agents needs to take into account factors which increase the "effect size", such as dosage, treatment duration, the use of two-phase trials, and pattern analysis of responders. Although many patients are thought to receive inadequate doses of antidepressants, relatively few dose-response studies have been performed. However, trials of both tricyclic antidepressants and phenelzine have shown that statistically significant improvements in outcome result from the use of higher dosages; the length of treatment may also affect results. In some studies, the proportion of patients showing a clear-cut response increased significantly among patients treated with active drug instead of placebo when the treatment period was extended from 4 to 6 weeks, independent of the dose used. There may thus be a distinct advantage in extending trials of antidepressants for a minimum of 6 weeks. Two-phase drug trials can be used to extend the trial period still further in responding patients, to emphasize the contrast between treatment and placebo effects and to eliminate type-2 errors. Twelve-week trials might increase the statistical power of the evaluation by 10-20%, in studies where the drug effect size is small. Pattern analysis of the timing and duration of patients' responses has been shown to aid the distinction of true responses from non-specific or placebo effects, and may be useful for evaluating data from studies of antidepressant agents which yield ambiguous results.

screening.rationale: Paper was a methodological review of antidepressant trial design that discussed placebo-related issues (placebo response, trial duration, two-phase designs, pattern analysis) making placebo science a main subject.

classification.summary: Reviewed methodological factors in antidepressant trials and highlighted dose, treatment duration, two-phase designs, and pattern analysis to distinguish drug effects from placebo responses.

title: Caffeine tolerance and choice in humans.
abstract: Thirty-two healthy subjects with histories of moderate caffeine consumption abstained from dietary caffeine throughout the study. Subjects were stratified into two groups based on several factors including caffeine preference, which was assessed using a caffeine versus placebo choice procedure. Subsequently, subjects received either caffeine (300 mg t.i.d.) or placebo (placebo t.i.d.) for 18 consecutive days, and thereafter were exposed again to a caffeine versus placebo choice procedure. The study documented tolerance development to the subjective effects of caffeine: after chronic dosing, administration of caffeine produced significant subjective effects in the chronic placebo group but not in the chronic caffeine group. The study also provided indirect evidence for tolerance development: during chronic dosing, the chronic caffeine and placebo groups did not differ meaningfully on ratings of mood and subjective effect. When subjects were categorized into caffeine choosers or nonchoosers, caffeine choosers tended to report positive subjective effects of caffeine and negative subjective effects of placebo. Nonchoosers, in contrast, tended to report negative subjective effects of caffeine. Chronic caffeine did not alter the reinforcing effects of caffeine as assessed by caffeine versus placebo choice, possibly because the relatively short duration of caffeine abstinence in the placebo condition was not sufficient to result in maximal withdrawal effects after termination of the relatively high caffeine dose. This study provides the clearest evidence to date of complete tolerance development to a CNS effect of caffeine in humans.

screening.rationale: Empirical randomized study that analyzed subjective responses to placebo versus caffeine and used a placebo-versus-caffeine choice procedure, thus examining placebo/sham responses and reinforcing effects rather than using placebo solely as an inert comparator for drug efficacy.

classification.summary: Randomized 32 healthy adults to chronic caffeine or placebo for 18 days and compared caffeine versus placebo choice and subjective effects, finding tolerance to caffeine's subjective effects in the chronic caffeine group.
classification.key_finding: Found that after chronic dosing, caffeine produced significant subjective effects in the chronic-placebo group but not in the chronic-caffeine group, indicating tolerance.

title: Conditioned responses to cocaine-related stimuli in cocaine abuse patients.
abstract: Subjects with a history of free-basing and smoking cocaine but no history of opiate injections were exposed to three sets of stimuli. They received cocaine-related stimuli in one session, opiate-related stimuli in a second session, and non-drug stimuli on a third occasion. Compared to the opiate and non-drug cues, the cocaine-related events caused reliable decreases in skin temperature and skin resistance, and reliable increases in heart rate, self-reported cocaine craving, and self-reported cocaine withdrawal. Furthermore, control subjects lacking a history of cocaine or opiate use failed to show such differential responding. These results suggest that cocaine-related stimuli evoke Pavlovian conditioned responses in cocaine abuse patients. Such findings encourage continuing efforts to develop drug treatment strategies based on conditioning principles.

screening.rationale: The study experimentally tested Pavlovian conditioned responses to drug-related versus neutral cues in cocaine-abusing patients, addressing classical conditioning mechanisms relevant to placebo/nocebo/context effects (inclusion rule for conditioning studies).

classification.summary: Exposed cocaine-dependent patients to cocaine, opiate, and neutral cues and found cue-specific increases in heart rate and craving and decreases in skin temperature and skin resistance, indicating Pavlovian conditioned responses to cocaine cues.
classification.key_finding: Cocaine-related cues reliably increased heart rate and craving and decreased skin temperature and skin resistance compared with opiate and neutral cues.

title: The ethics of placebos in AIDS drug trials.
journal: HEC forum : an interdisciplinary journal on hospitals' ethical and legal issues

screening.rationale: Paper's title and MeSH terms indicate it is a review addressing the ethics of placebo use in AIDS clinical trials, meeting the 'placebo science' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical issues and debates surrounding use of placebo controls in AIDS/HIV drug trials, focusing on research design, consent, and justice.
